sections.report:
**First read:** The eye lands on "Before you board" (bold, about 40 px, at x120 y108–148). Next it hits three paragraphs set entirely in capitals, which read like a dense block of shouting. It's a page of practical notes for river-ferry passengers. It feels plain and neutral, with a lot of empty white space below and to the right.

**Job (assumed):** An information page that tells ferry passengers the timetable, the bicycle rules and the winter changes before they travel.

**Walk: The whole piece**
- One-sentence purpose: yes.
- Main image and headline make one idea: yes. There's no image, so the line doesn't apply.
- Every element does a job: yes. The eyebrow, heading and three paragraphs each carry something, and there's no ornament.
- One mood and era: yes. The body is all caps, but that's a type-setting issue that belongs in the Text section. Type and colours are otherwise one consistent sans-serif system.
- Copy finished: yes. There's no placeholder text and no misspellings.
- Same kind of element looks the same: yes. The three paragraphs are styled identically.
- Colours, shapes and directions suit the mood: yes. It's neutral and calm, which fits practical notes.
- Each heading names its section: yes. "Before you board" covers the timetable, bicycles and winter, all things to know before travelling.

No line came out `no` or `unsure`, so there are no entries to open.

---

**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **Purpose is clear at once.** The label "PASSENGER NOTES" over "Before you board" tells a first-time viewer within a second that this is practical information for ferry passengers, before they read the body.
- **The copy is concrete.** Each paragraph states who does what and when: "every forty minutes", "about twelve minutes in calm weather", "wheel them on after foot passengers have boarded", "one boat each hour". A passenger can act on it without filling in gaps.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 8 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

It then goes up to the small grey "PASSENGER NOTES" label, then into three body paragraphs set in all capitals (y≈178–428). It reads as an information page for ferry passengers, and it feels calm but shouted in the body. My assumption about the job: a short notice that tells ferry passengers the schedule and the rules before they travel.

What matters first:

- Distinct text levels, no near-equal sizes? yes. There are three levels: the label (about 13 px, bold, tracked, grey), the title (about 40 px, bold), and the body (about 18 px, regular). The steps between them are large.
- Headings differ from the text by more than size? yes. The title is bold against regular body. The label differs from the body by size, weight, tracking and grey colour, even though both are in capitals.

No line came out no or unsure, so there were no entries to open.

---

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- The title "Before you board" (x≈120–420, y≈108–148) is the only large, bold element on the page. It's about twice the body size and much heavier, so the eye knows at once where to start and what the page is about.
- The label "PASSENGER NOTES" (y≈76–90) sits a clear step below the body. It's small, bold, letterspaced and grey, so it reads as a category tag and doesn't compete with the title. It also stays distinct from the all-caps body because of its size, weight and colour. Keep those three differences if the body case changes.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

sections.report:
**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
None.

On three lines I was unsure at first. After reading the entries, all three are yes:
- **Empty space.** All of the empty space is in one L-shaped area: about 400 px to the right of the column (x≈875–1280) and about 370 px below the last paragraph (y≈430–800). It is not spread thin between the elements, so it meets "White space is gathered, not scattered" (Ruder).
- **Balance.** All the weight sits in the top-left, but this is a short reading page that starts at the top-left, and the space below is just where the content ends. Nothing tips the page.
- **Proportion.** The column's right edge at about x≈875 is set by the text measure, not by an arbitrary split of the frame.

The line length is long for all-caps text, at roughly 85–90 characters. That belongs to the Text section, not this one.

**What's working.**
- Everything starts at one left edge, x≈120: the eyebrow "PASSENGER NOTES", the heading, and all three paragraphs. With no near-misses, the column reads as one deliberate block.
- The spacing shows the groups. Lines within a paragraph are about 27 px apart and paragraphs about 47 px apart. The eyebrow sits tight above the heading, and the heading is closer to the body than to the top margin. So the three notes read as three separate points under one title.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 13 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Is every sentence or paragraph set in mixed case, with capitals kept to short headings and labels? No.** All three body paragraphs are set entirely in capitals: about x 120–872, y 178–428, eight lines and roughly 75 words. Capitals have no ascenders or descenders, so words lose their shapes and become rectangles of the same height. The reader has to spell their way through the text instead of recognising words. The block also reads as one flat grey slab, so nothing shows the reader where the useful facts are: every forty minutes, twelve minutes per crossing, bicycles free, one boat an hour in winter. Since the type is plain and dark, this is the main thing slowing the reader down. The capitals are also set at about the face's default spacing. Capitals in running text want extra space, so this makes them denser still, but the real fix is to stop using capitals here, not to space them out. Source: Butterick, *Practical Typography*, "All caps" ("Don't capitalize whole paragraphs"); Hochuli, *Detail in Typography* (capitals are "particularly difficult to read"). Fix: set the paragraphs in upper and lower case. Keep capitals for short labels like the "PASSENGER NOTES" eyebrow, which is already handled well. Mark: convention, and a defect in what it costs the reader. Weight: major.

**What's working.** The rest of the setting is sound. The body looks about 17 px with leading of about 1.6, and lines run about 68–72 characters, so the measure and line spacing suit reading once the case is fixed. The eyebrow "PASSENGER NOTES" is used the right way: a small, bold, letterspaced, mid-grey label, clearly secondary to the tight, heavy heading "Before you board". Together they make a clean two-level header in one family.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 29 yes, 1 no (every sentence in mixed case)

sections.report:
The piece is achromatic (white ground, near-black heading and body, one cool mid-gray eyebrow at x≈120, y≈83), so I'm walking the color lines from what the whole image shows. The image is 1280×800, small enough that no crops were needed.

**First read.** The eye lands on the bold "Before you board" heading at the top left, then drops into three paragraphs set in all caps that read as one block. It reads as a ferry passenger information page: calm, plain and grayscale.

**Walk (Color)**
- Small palette: yes. White, near-black and one cool gray, with no hue at all.
- Saturated color kept to a small share: yes. There isn't any.
- Clear value range that holds in grayscale: yes. Near-black on white, with the gray eyebrow as a middle step.
- Warm forward, cool recedes: yes. There are no hues. The cool gray eyebrow sits back, which suits a label.
- Matching colors look the same: yes. The heading and body read as the same near-black throughout.
- No vibrating edges: yes.
- Status colors used for their usual meaning: yes. There are none.
- Color never carries meaning alone: yes. Nothing is coded by color.
- Dark theme background is dark gray: yes. This is not a dark theme.

Every line is yes, so there are no entries to open.

**Section.** Color: applies. The piece is achromatic, and that choice is itself what gets judged here.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.** 
- **Value does all the structural work.** The page uses only near-black on white plus one mid-gray step for the "PASSENGER NOTES" eyebrow (x≈120, y≈76–90). The label sits clearly below the heading without adding a hue, so the page would look exactly the same in grayscale. For a plain notice page that is the right amount of color.
- **No hue competes for attention.** With nothing saturated on the page, the dark, bold heading is the strongest mark, and it is the right one to be strongest.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Findings**
None.
